extracted.intended_audience: Title IX coordinators, school administrators, institutional legal counsel, and K-12 and higher-education compliance officers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements for handling Title IX formal complaints, with emphasis on evidence production, investigative reports, privacy protections, timelines, and procedural safeguards for hearings. Applies to recipients (schools, colleges, universities) implementing §106.45 grievance processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties' right to inspect and review evidence directly related to allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must be given the opportunity to inspect and review any evidence obtained as part of an investigation that is directly related to the allegations raised in a formal complaint (§106.45(b)(5)(vi)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to help parties adequately prepare for a hearing. Only evidence 'directly related to' the allegations must be shared. Recipients cannot exclude evidence an investigator intends to use in the investigative report. This disclosure aligns with FERPA's approach to records that directly relate to a student. Recipients may provide electronic or hard-copy access and must ensure equal opportunity to inspect and review for both parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on accessing treatment/medical/counseling records without voluntary written consent
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient cannot access, consider, disclose, or otherwise use a party's records made or maintained by a physician, psychiatrist, psychologist, or other recognized professional or paraprofessional in connection with treatment unless the recipient obtains the party's voluntary, written consent (§106.45(b)(5)(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restriction applies even where HIPAA or State-law equivalents do not apply. If the party is not an 'eligible student' under FERPA, the recipient must obtain voluntary written consent of a parent as defined in 34 CFR 99.3. Parties are not required to provide such medical records to the recipient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit disclosure to evidence 'directly related to' the allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must provide 'any evidence obtained as part of the investigation that is directly related to the allegations raised in a formal complaint.' Evidence that is not directly related need not be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must review all evidence and determine what is directly related. Recipients have discretion to interpret 'directly related,' consistent with FERPA practice. Examples: attendance or academic records are discoverable only if directly related to the allegations (e.g., missed classes caused by harassment). Lay persons (not only attorneys) may make relevance determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of legally recognized privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient's grievance process must not require, allow, rely upon, or otherwise use questions or evidence that constitute, or seek disclosure of, information protected under a legally recognized privilege, unless the person holding such privilege has waived the privilege (added §106.45(b)(1)(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney-client privileged materials need not be shared. If the privilege holder waives privilege voluntarily, the materials may be shared. The regulation avoids incorporating additional complex privilege regimes by reference; it expressly protects privileged information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum ten-day periods for response and receipt of investigative report before hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties must have at least ten days to submit a written response to evidence directly related to the allegations, and must receive the investigative report at least ten days prior to a hearing (§106.45(b)(5)(vi)-(vii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department does not define whether 'days' are calendar, business, or school days; recipients may choose. Recipients may give more than ten days. If the investigative report is not ready at least ten days before the hearing, the recipient should delay the hearing; failing to provide the ten days is a violation even if parties purport to waive the requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted measures to limit copying/dissemination must be applied equally
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may use file-sharing platforms that restrict parties and advisors from downloading or copying evidence and may prohibit photographing or public dissemination of evidence, as long as measures apply equally to both parties (§106.45(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such measures can address sensitive materials (e.g., photographs with nudity). Recipients retain discretion to select reasonable measures to enable response/use of evidence at a hearing while preventing impermissible use. Recipients may require parties to agree not to photograph or copy evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department will not require HIPAA-level data-security standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to require recipients to adopt a data-security standard benchmarked to HIPAA or to incorporate HIPAA by reference in these Title IX regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients that are covered entities under HIPAA must still comply with HIPAA. The Department encourages secure data systems but will not create overlapping federal data-security obligations; recipients must comply with any other laws that apply to them and are best positioned to determine applicable obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic or hard-copy delivery of evidence and investigative report
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient may provide a party and the party's advisor either a hard copy of the evidence and investigative report or the materials in an electronic format; recipients are not required to provide hard-copy only access (§106.45(b)(5)(vi)-(vii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing electronic delivery permits 'view-only' access platforms. Recipients should consider access limitations (e.g., students lacking computers or internet) and provide accommodations. Nothing prevents providing both formats. Recipients may provide supervised access but should be cautious not to impede parties from privately consulting advisors; parties can prevent advisor access if they choose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative report must fairly summarize relevant evidence; investigator must not determine responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The investigative report must fairly summarize relevant evidence (§106.45(b)(5)(vii)). The Department declines to prescribe specific required contents beyond this fair summary; however, an investigator must not be the decision-maker regarding responsibility (§106.45(b)(7)(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may include facts and interview statements; if including a credibility analysis, ensure it does not amount to a determination of responsibility. Decision-makers (not investigators) should make responsibility determinations; investigators should avoid crossing that line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation of formal complaints arising from same facts or circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may consolidate formal complaints where the allegations of sexual harassment arise out of the same facts or circumstances (§106.45(b)(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consolidated complaints mean the allegations directly relate to all parties; recipients must issue the same written determination regarding responsibility to all parties simultaneously and may not redact any part. If complaints are not consolidated, separate written determinations are required for each formal complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal access to evidence for advisors; recipient may not refuse advisor access if party chooses
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may not refuse to provide evidence or the investigative report to a party's advisor of choice if the party wants the advisor to have access; conversely, if a party does not want an advisor to have materials, the recipient should honor that request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients cannot deny a party's chosen advisor access; this supports parties' ability to prepare and consult. Recipients should balance this with appropriate protections against dissemination when requested by the party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX Coordinator must not restrict parties from submitting evidence or influence submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: A Title IX Coordinator should not encourage or discourage a party from submitting evidence; restricting a party from providing evidence could violate the regulations and indicate bias or conflict of interest (§106.45(b)(1)(iii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinators must inform parties they will have opportunity to inspect and review evidence. Any improper restriction may constitute a regulatory violation and raise concerns about impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of prior sexual behavior/predisposition generally barred with narrow exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(6) prohibits all evidence (not just questions) about the complainant's sexual behavior or predisposition unless such evidence is offered to prove that someone other than the respondent committed the conduct alleged or to prove consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a recipient obtains such evidence that is directly related to the allegations, both parties must have equal opportunity to inspect and review it to prepare to respond or object to its inclusion in the investigative report and at the hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients should not obtain evidence that cannot legally be shared
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of these regulations, a recipient should not obtain as part of an investigation any evidence directly relating to the allegations that cannot legally be shared with the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access to certain medical, counseling, or other records may be governed by other federal or state laws that typically require party consent. Recipients do not have subpoena power to obtain medical records from covered entities without consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reasonable accommodations for students with disabilities in accessing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are encouraged and required to provide whatever reasonable accommodations are necessary for students with disabilities while complying with these regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider accessibility of digital formats, ability to view materials outside of recipient operating hours, and other adjustments to ensure meaningful access to evidence and investigative reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department retains recipient discretion on many procedural elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department does not prescribe all procedural details; recipients determine supportive measures, standard of evidence, how to weigh evidence, sanctions, remedies, and many operational choices regarding evidence sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While recipients have discretion, they must still comply with specific regulatory mandates (e.g., ten-day periods, access rights, protections for privileged and treatment records). The Department declined to mandate a single method for preventing copying or to adopt a uniform technological approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with FERPA — no inherent conflict; Title IX obligations not obviated by FERPA
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department states there is no inherent conflict between these Title IX regulations and FERPA; FERPA allows disclosure of records directly related to a particular student in the context of due process. §106.6(e) clarifies that the obligation to comply with these regulations is 'not obviated or alleviated by the FERPA statute.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients subject to FERPA should apply the 'directly related to' test consistently with FERPA practice. The Department has previously interpreted FERPA to permit disclosure of witness statements directly related to the student when segregation/redaction would destroy meaning. In cases of direct conflict that impair Title IX's primary purpose, Title IX requirements control.
